title: China’s central bank moves liquidity operations overnight as domestic demand lags
summary: China’s third-quarter monetary policy report explains why the People’s Bank of China wants to keep financing conditions easy despite faster industrial price inflation. The Bank describes stronger supply than demand and an uneven recovery in domestic spending. Real GDP rose 4.6% year on year over the first nine months. Consumer prices rose 0.9% over that period, or 1.1% excluding food and energy. Producer prices rose 2.3% over nine months and 5.0% in September alone, partly reflecting raw materials costs and strong demand for electronics. The Bank retained its moderately loose stance and called for stronger countercyclical support. Its proposals address where financing is available and how quickly market rates transmit to borrowers. The report gives no date or size for a further general rate cut (pp. 39–42, 47–50).

The clearest change for the money market concerns the rate the Bank can control each trading day. It gradually introduced overnight reverse repos around month ends and tax dates during the quarter. From 2 November, overnight operations were offered each working day at a fixed 1.25%, with participants bidding for quantities. Seven-day operations switched to fixed amounts and multiple-price interest-rate tenders, mainly around dates of elevated funding needs. The third-quarter average for DR001, the overnight secured funding rate among depository institutions, was 1.38%. Chart 1 shows that this traded rate had already been fluctuating close to the central bank’s short-term operation rate. Wider use of floating-rate loans linked to DR001 could extend that influence to companies. How much borrowing actually reprices against it will determine the strength of that channel (pp. 1–2, 14, 23–24, 49).

Credit growth and credit prices give different readings of demand. At end-September the stock of aggregate financing to the real economy was RMB468.17tn, up 7.1% year on year. Of RMB27.46tn in additional financing in the first nine months, RMB11.5tn came from renminbi bank loans to the real economy and RMB10.3tn from net government bond financing. New corporate loans in September carried a weighted average rate of 2.96%, down 19 basis points from a year earlier. The availability of cheap credit need not translate into new private investment. The Bank increased the technology and equipment-upgrade relending quota by RMB200bn, raising its funding share from 60% to 100%, and cut the pledged supplementary lending rate by 25 basis points to 1.5%. These are targeted funding terms and capacity. Actual take-up and completed expenditure must be measured separately (pp. 2–4, 8, 19–20, Tables 1 and 4).

A separate facility announced in October addresses the possibility that redemptions force bond funds to sell into a falling market. Under the mechanism in Box 3, eligible systemically important institutions borrow central bank bills, raise cash against them in the repo market and buy eligible assets or units from affected products. They must repay the Bank and remain responsible for gains or losses. Collateral standards, haircuts and fair pricing limit public exposure. The facility is intended for widespread redemption stress and is to be withdrawn as liquidity normalises. It does not absorb an individual fund’s credit losses. That distinction matters when pricing illiquid bonds or assessing a fund’s ability to raise immediate cash (pp. 15–17).

Market prices during the quarter give a baseline for evaluating those changes. From end-June to end-September, the one-year government yield rose 10 basis points to 1.22%, while the ten-year yield fell five to 1.68%. The spread narrowed to 46 basis points. These observations in Chart 4 precede the November operating change. They cannot isolate its effect or establish what future easing investors had priced. The renminbi also appreciated against both the dollar and the CFETS basket from end-2025 to end-September. The Bank retained a managed float, with attention to excessive exchange-rate moves and cross-border flows. It gave no exchange-rate objective in levels (pp. 12–13, 29, 49–50).

questions.question: Will the overnight liquidity framework lower and stabilise the borrowing costs that firms actually pay?
questions.detail: The report describes a fixed-price daily tender, an overnight market rate already close to the central bank rate and initial loans linked to DR001. It gives no share of outstanding credit that resets on that basis. Track China Foreign Exchange Trade System overnight rates through tax dates, compare the spread to broader repo rates and examine new-loan benchmark choices in bank disclosures. Persistent changes in spreads and repricing frequencies would matter more for short rates and bank margins than a single quiet fixing.

questions.question: Is targeted credit creating additional investment or refinancing existing projects?
questions.detail: The Bank expanded relending quotas while aggregate financing included a large government contribution. Lower quoted rates and larger quotas provide no direct measure of completed private expenditure. Compare subsequent drawings under the facilities and corporate medium- and long-term loan flows with National Bureau of Statistics equipment and private investment data. This would help distinguish better access to credit from a durable rise in demand, with different implications for industrial earnings and bond yields.

questions.question: How much of a bond fund’s redemption risk can the new facility absorb in stressed markets?
questions.detail: Box 3 specifies the financing chain, eligibility and allocation of losses, but gives no realised capacity for a particular portfolio. Compare future central bank operating notices with fund holdings, available eligible collateral, redemption terms and market repo haircuts. Holders of lower-rated bonds need to know whether the assets they own can raise cash in stress or still have to be sold into thin markets.
